name: Porto
tagline: A river city of tiles, bridges and a famous wedding

lessons.title: The station painted in blue
lessons.hook: Step into the entrance hall. Its walls hold about 20,000 hand-painted tiles, and they tell Portugal's story like a giant comic book.
lessons.challenge: One of the big tile panels shows a Portuguese prince conquering a city in North Africa. Which city?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player names Ceuta, the North African city taken by Portugal in 1415.
hints: Look for the panel full of soldiers, ships and a prince on horseback.
It's a port city on the African side of the Strait of Gibraltar, still Spanish today.
lessons.story: The tiles (azulejos) were painted by Jorge Colaço and finished around 1916, when the station opened on the site of an old convent. The panel you found shows the conquest of Ceuta in 1415, the first step of Portugal's Age of Discovery. Prince Henry, later called 'the Navigator', fought there. He was born right here in Porto.

lessons.title: A church built like a castle
lessons.hook: Walk around the cathedral and look at its top edge. It doesn't look much like a church from out here.
lessons.challenge: The roofline has battlements, like a castle. What does that tell you the building was also meant for?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player says the cathedral was also built to defend or protect the city, as a fortress, against attack or war. Reward any reasonable phrasing in any language.
hints: Battlements were where defenders stood behind the gaps in the wall.
Think about medieval Porto: what did a strong building on a hilltop need to survive?
lessons.story: Begun in the 12th century, the Sé was a fortress church on Porto's highest hill, meant to protect as well as to pray. In 1387 it hosted a famous wedding: King João I married the English princess Philippa of Lancaster here, sealing the alliance between Portugal and England — still the oldest diplomatic alliance in the world. Their son was Prince Henry the Navigator.

lessons.title: The bridge from Eiffel's workshop
lessons.hook: From the riverside, look up at the huge iron arch spanning the Douro.
lessons.challenge: Count them: how many decks (levels you can cross on) does the bridge have?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player says the bridge has two decks (an upper and a lower one).
hints: Look for people crossing high up as well as right by the water.
One deck carries the metro on top; the other carries cars near the river.
lessons.story: The bridge opened in 1886. It was designed by Théophile Seyrig, a former partner of Gustave Eiffel — the Eiffel Tower came three years later. Its iron arch was, at the time, the longest of its kind in the world. Today the upper deck carries the metro and walkers, and the lower deck links Ribeira to the port wine cellars of Gaia.

lessons.title: The tower sailors steered by
lessons.hook: Find the slender Baroque tower that rises above the rooftops. For a long time, ships coming up the river used it as a landmark.
lessons.challenge: The tower was designed by an Italian architect who spent most of his life in Porto. What was his surname?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player names Nicolau (Niccolò) Nasoni. Accept spelling mistakes.
hints: He was born in Tuscany and worked on many Porto churches.
lessons.story: Nicolau Nasoni came from Tuscany, settled in Porto and shaped its Baroque look. The tower was built between 1754 and 1763 and is about 75 metres tall. For many years it was the tallest building in Portugal and a guide for ships on the Douro. Nasoni asked to be buried in the Clérigos church at its foot.

lessons.title: Myth or history?
lessons.hook: Stand across the street from the bookshop and look at its white neo-Gothic front. No ticket needed for this one.
lessons.challenge: Two painted figures flank the upper window. What two ideas do they represent?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player says the figures represent Art and Science (in any order or language). Half-right answers naming one of them should get encouraging feedback but are not correct.
hints: One is about creating beauty, the other about knowledge.
Think of the two things a great bookshop sells: stories and facts.
lessons.story: The Lello brothers opened this shop in 1906, and the figures of Art and Science on its front were painted by José Bielman. Many visitors come because they've heard it inspired Harry Potter. J.K. Rowling has said she never visited it. That makes this a good lesson in itself: a famous story isn't always a true one, so check the source.

lessons.title: The house between two churches
lessons.hook: Find the two churches standing side by side — one with a huge blue-and-white tiled wall. They look joined, but they aren't.
lessons.challenge: Look closely at the gap between the two churches. What's hidden there?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player says there is a very narrow house (a building people lived in) between the two churches.
hints: The gap isn't empty — it has windows and a door.
It's only about a metre wide, and people lived in it.
lessons.story: Between the Carmelitas church (for nuns) and the Carmo church (for friars) sits a house barely a metre wide. The usual explanation is that the two churches were not allowed to share a wall, keeping nuns and friars apart — and people lived in the narrow house until the 20th century. The big tile panel on the Carmo's side wall was added in 1912.

lessons.title: The bridge of boats
lessons.hook: On the Ribeira riverside, near the old bridge, look for a small bronze memorial on the wall where people often leave candles and flowers.
lessons.challenge: It remembers a disaster on a bridge made of boats. In what year did it happen?
hints: It happened while Napoleon's army was invading Portugal.
The early 1800s — the year the French marshal Soult took Porto.
lessons.story: On 29 March 1809, French troops under Marshal Soult attacked Porto. Crowds fled across the Ponte das Barcas, a bridge made of boats tied together over the Douro. It gave way under the weight, and a great many people drowned — estimates run into the thousands. The bronze 'Alminhas da Ponte' still gets candles today, more than two centuries later.
